news.headline: First tranche of India-US trade deal finalised, legal drafting under process, says Piyush Goyal
news.story_lead: First tranche of India-US trade deal finalised, legal drafting under process, says Piyush Goyal Piyush Goyal also said FTA between India and the European Union will be inked in December and would come into force from February or March next year. The final tranche of India-US bilateral trade agreement is ready and legal drafting is currently under process, Union minister for commerce and industry Piyush Goyal said on Thursday. He said the deal will be operationalised once a ‘comparable or competitive advantage over our peer countries’ is achieved.
news.full_article_text: First tranche of India-US trade deal finalised, legal drafting under process, says Piyush Goyal Piyush Goyal also said FTA between India and the European Union will be inked in December and would come into force from February or March next year. The final tranche of India-US bilateral trade agreement is ready and legal drafting is currently under process, Union minister for commerce and industry Piyush Goyal said on Thursday. He said the deal will be operationalised once a ‘comparable or competitive advantage over our peer countries’ is achieved. “The US bilateral trade agreement's first tranche has been finalised. It's going through the final contours, the legal drafting, and we hope to be able to finalize that soon and operationalise it once we get a comparable or competitive advantage over our peer countries,” Goyal said. Also read: Sensex shoots up over 1,500 points, closes at three-week high: Why were markets up today? The update from Goyal on the trade negotiations came over a week after finance minister Nirmala Sitharaman said the talks on the trade deal have reached a "plateau". He also said that the free trade agreement between India and the European Union will be inked in December and would come into force from February or March next year. Later Commerce Secretary Rajesh Agrawal said that the negotiations on the US trade pact are moving in the right direction. Meanwhile, US Ambassador to India, Sergio Gor also said bilateral trade negotiations were moving at an "incredible pace", and the "big items are done", underlining that he was confident that both sides will get the pact through, according to news agency PTI. Also read: 'Racist hostility', 'anti-India hate': India on 'attempted mass shooting' targeting Hindu temple in US “I won't like to get into too many details at this stage, and let the ministers announce that. But in the grand scheme of things, big items are done,” Gor was quoted as saying. "We're actively engaged... Within three weeks of arriving here, we announced a trade deal. The European Union trade deal took almost 20 years. So we're at an incredible pace, and I am confident that we will get it done," Gor said. Earlier on Tuesday, external affairs minister S Jaishankar said that India and the US are continuing to engage to iron out differences on the proposed trade deal, and negotiations are heading towards a “landing point”. He noted that the core fundamentals of the bilateral strategic partnership remain unchanged, news agency PTI reported. "I think we are waiting on a few things. I wouldn't be comfortable spilling the beans in public," he was quoted as saying. "I think we are waiting on a few things. I wouldn't be comfortable spilling the beans in public," he said at the Bloomberg New Economy Forum on Tuesday evening when asked about the status of the negotiations between the two sides. - ABOUT THE AUTHOR Sana Fazili Sana started her career in 2018 with News18 and later moved to BoomLive. In the meantime, she thought it was a good idea to share what she learnt, hence took up part-time teaching of journalism course at Jamia Millia Islamia, which she says, she thoroughly enjoyed-not sure if the feeling was mutual. For a year, she also tried her hands at communication roles, only to realise she was more comfortable with news. So, joined HT in September 2025. Not much of a talker, always up for chai and sarcasm. news.headline: No coercive action against woman journalist on Delhi cop’s complaint, orders Supreme Court
news.story_lead: No coercive action against woman journalist on Delhi cop’s complaint, orders Supreme Court The Supreme Court directed no coercive action against a journalist accused of casteist remarks against a Delhi ACP after she alleged sexual harassment by the officer. news.full_article_text: No coercive action against woman journalist on Delhi cop’s complaint, orders Supreme Court The Supreme Court directed no coercive action against a journalist accused of casteist remarks against a Delhi ACP after she alleged sexual harassment by the officer. The Supreme Court on Thursday directed that no coercive action be taken against a woman journalist facing allegations of making casteist remarks against Assistant Commissioner of Police (ACP) Vivek Bhagat, after she claimed that the complaint was a counterblast to her allegations of sexual harassment against the same police officer during protests in the Capital. The order was passed on a day when the Delhi high court declined to urgently hear the woman journalist’s plea challenging the case against her for allegedly making casteist remarks against ACP Bhagat, publicly humiliating him and obstructing him from discharging his official duties. A bench of Chief Justice of India (CJI) Surya Kant and Justice Joymalya Bagchi took up the case of the woman journalist while issuing notice on a petition filed by the Network of Women in Media, India (NWMI), which highlighted instances of violence and sexual harassment faced by women journalists while covering protests in the Capital on October 10 and before that. Deep Dive The petitioner, represented by senior advocate Indira Jaising, was allowed to submit in a sealed cover the identities of all women journalists who were victims and wished to submit their complaints in writing. Jaising said that since the allegation by the woman journalist was against police personnel, an independent commission should be constituted, comprising predominantly former women judges, Indian Police Service (IPS) officers, eminent citizens and social activists. The court said, “Meanwhile, no coercive action be taken against the journalist,” and further allowed Jaising to submit in a sealed cover her suggestions on persons who could be part of the committee to look into the allegations. “There are allegations against certain police officers. We are considering whether there must be an independent committee to probe them,” the court remarked. The bench said, “Journalists will require an extra category of protection. There are two rights involved – right to free speech and right to practice profession. But we must also keep in mind whether anybody with a mike and mobile can claim to be a journalist.” The court said that there were accredited journalists, persons employed as journalists with news organisations, freelance journalists and influencers. “There has to be a detailed examination whether freedom of speech and expression right contained in Article 19(1)(a) of the Constitution empowers every citizen to be a journalist.” Solicitor general Tushar Mehta, appearing for the police, told the court to await its response before taking any decision on constituting an independent commission. On the allegation made by the woman journalist against the officer, Mehta said, “Difficulty is that in the present era of mobile technology, everybody is a journalist. I am not on this lady but there is a version that the video she has produced (alleging harassment) could be AI generated.” Jaising said that a standard operating procedure must be in place, as women journalists faced no obstacles while covering events in war zones but faced violence and harassment while covering protests at Jantar Mantar. “There is no national protocol on how to deal with such cases. We do not want any coercive action to be taken against any woman journalist alleging harassment.” Mehta said that a blanket order of no coercive action could not be passed. “No lady should be inappropriately dealt with, including the female police personnel. There are allegations of harassment faced by them. Passing an order of no FIR against lady journalists will be too wide a relief.” Senior advocate Gaurav Bhatia, appearing in one of the petitions, submitted to the court that on October 12, when Leader of Opposition Rahul Gandhi, along with other Opposition leaders, stormed into the precincts of the Supreme Court with a huge gathering of lawyers, a woman journalist who was three months pregnant was pushed by Gandhi. She suffered injuries and had to be hospitalised. Mehta also said that it was strange that Jaising was not raising the concern of this woman journalist. Jaising accused Bhatia of trying to “bring politics” into the case, even as the court remarked, “We cannot take suo motu cognisance on an oral submission. If there is a petition, we will examine.” Earlier in the day, the Delhi high court bench of acting Chief Justice Nitin Sambre and Justice Sanjay Sharma, which took up the matter of the woman journalist alleging harassment by ACP Bhagat, turned down her lawyer’s request for an urgent hearing on Thursday. However, the bench agreed to hear the matter on Friday. The FIR, seen by HT and registered on Tuesday, booked the journalist and two others under sections 221 (obstructing public servant), 356(2) (defamation) and 3(5) (joint liability) of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS), alongside provisions under the Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act. The petition stated that the FIR was a “pure misuse of power” by the police authorities and a counterblast to the October 3 complaint at Parliament Street police station. “The said allegations are baseless, devoid of merit and actuated by mala fides, being a clear counterblast to the complaint of sexual assault lodged by the Petitioner against the Respondent No. 2, so as to dissuade, extort, humiliate and intimidate the petitioner,” the petition said. It added that the 10-day delay in reporting the alleged incident, juxtaposed with the registration of the impugned FIR within half an hour of the information being supplied, while Delhi Police had not registered an FIR based on her allegations, raised serious concerns regarding the bona fides of the police authorities. The controversy dates to October 3, when the woman journalist said she was recording the detention of a Left activist at the protest when Bhagat allegedly touched her inappropriately and pushed her. Bhagat denied the allegations. The police forwarded her complaint to the crime branch for an “impartial inquiry”.

The Supreme Court on Thursday directed that no coercive action be taken against a woman journalist facing allegations of making casteist remarks against Assistant Commissioner of Police (ACP) Vivek Bhagat, after she claimed that the complaint was a counterblast to her allegations of sexual harassment against the same police officer during protests in the Capital.

The order was passed on a day when the Delhi high court declined to urgently hear the woman journalist’s plea challenging the case against her for allegedly making casteist remarks against ACP Bhagat, publicly humiliating him and obstructing him from discharging his official duties.

A bench of Chief Justice of India (CJI) Surya Kant and Justice Joymalya Bagchi took up the case of the woman journalist while issuing notice on a petition filed by the Network of Women in Media, India (NWMI), which highlighted instances of violence and sexual harassment faced by women journalists while covering protests in the Capital on October 10 and before that.

The petitioner, represented by senior advocate Indira Jaising, was allowed to submit in a sealed cover the identities of all women journalists who were victims and wished to submit their complaints in writing.

Jaising said that since the allegation by the woman journalist was against police personnel, an independent commission should be constituted, comprising predominantly former women judges, Indian Police Service (IPS) officers, eminent citizens and social activists.

The court said, “Meanwhile, no coercive action be taken against the journalist,” and further allowed Jaising to submit in a sealed cover her suggestions on persons who could be part of the committee to look into the allegations. “There are allegations against certain police officers. We are considering whether there must be an independent committee to probe them,” the court remarked.

news.headline: US singer Mary Millben, CJP's Abhijeet Dipke trade barbs over 'foreign funding' amid anti-CEC protests in Delhi
news.story_lead: US singer Mary Millben, CJP's Abhijeet Dipke trade barbs over 'foreign funding' amid anti-CEC protests in Delhi Mary Millben and Abhijeet Dipke found themselves in a row on social media over the US singer's claims that CJP was funded by American donors. As the protests against Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar continue in India, Cockroach Janta Party founder Abhijeet Dipke found himself in a social media row with American singer Mary Millben. The American singer hit out at Dipke and the pressure group on Wednesday, alleging that the CJP was "funded by donors to the US" who are against Prime Minister Narendra Modi.
news.full_article_text: US singer Mary Millben, CJP's Abhijeet Dipke trade barbs over 'foreign funding' amid anti-CEC protests in Delhi Mary Millben and Abhijeet Dipke found themselves in a row on social media over the US singer's claims that CJP was funded by American donors. As the protests against Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar continue in India, Cockroach Janta Party founder Abhijeet Dipke found himself in a social media row with American singer Mary Millben. The American singer hit out at Dipke and the pressure group on Wednesday, alleging that the CJP was "funded by donors to the US" who are against Prime Minister Narendra Modi. Track LIVE updates on Delhi protest here "Do not fear, my young patriots. Your Prime Minister, who has served India for 25 years, 12 years as Prime Minister, elected three consecutive terms, is not going to bow to disruptive forces from my country. And these select donors have a pattern globally - target conservative global leaders, find an U.S. educated person from the country, radicalize them, send them back to the country, and fund them to start chaos and destruction. None of them have been successful but have impacted the development and governance of the country," the singer wrote on X. "It is time for a new voice in #India, born, raised, educated on the soil of India, to RISE UP, organise, and peacefully protest the disruptive spirit of the Cockroach Party... Rise up, young patriots! Rise up!," she added. Also Read | 'Agitations for a common cause': CJP's Dipke on INDIA bloc amid anti-CEC protests in Delhi Responding to Millben, Dipke took to X and asked: "Who gave foreign nationals the right to interfere in India's internal affairs?" "Why is Modi seeking the support of Americans to discredit his own countrymen? Who gave foreign nationals the right to interfere in India’s internal affairs? We are more than capable of dealing with our own issues. We don’t need outsiders interfering in our country’s affairs," the CJP founder wrote. The American singer, however, did not back down and hit out at Dipke yet again. "The truth sets everybody free. Even you. And here’s the truth: these US donors will drop you like a hot cake when you don’t succeed. And you won’t, because lawlessness never wins. Instead, take your U.S. education, talent, and use it for good. Sit down with PM Modi and be a positive voice to advance India. The truth of your courage to do what’s right lies in your next steps," the singer wrote. Millben added that Modi did not need American support because he has " 1.5 billion beautiful Indian citizens who support him and have for 25 years, 12 years as PM, three consecutive terms. And will again in 2029. That’s the truth." Mary Millben is a prominent African-American Hollywood actress and singer. She became a known name in India for her rendition of the national anthem and religious song 'Om Jai Jagdish Hare'. Millben also sang the Indian national anthem at an event in 2023 during OM Modi's visit to the US. This is not the first time the singer has supported PM Modi. On completion of his 25 years in public service, Millben described the prime minister as a “shining beacon of the Indian dream”. She also called for unity across communities to mark the milestone. As the protests against Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar continue in India, Cockroach Janta Party founder Abhijeet Dipke found himself in a social media row with American singer Mary Millben. The American singer hit out at Dipke and the pressure group on Wednesday, alleging that the CJP was "funded by donors to the US" who are against Prime Minister Narendra Modi. Track LIVE updates on Delhi protest here "Do not fear, my young patriots. Your Prime Minister, who has served India for 25 years, 12 years as Prime Minister, elected three consecutive terms, is not going to bow to disruptive forces from my country. And these select donors have a pattern globally - target conservative global leaders, find an U.S. educated person from the country, radicalize them, send them back to the country, and fund them to start chaos and destruction. None of them have been successful but have impacted the development and governance of the country," the singer wrote on X. "It is time for a new voice in #India, born, raised, educated on the soil of India, to RISE UP, organise, and peacefully protest the disruptive spirit of the Cockroach Party... Rise up, young patriots! Rise up!," she added. Also Read | 'Agitations for a common cause': CJP's Dipke on INDIA bloc amid anti-CEC protests in Delhi Responding to Millben, Dipke took to X and asked: "Who gave foreign nationals the right to interfere in India's internal affairs?" "Why is Modi seeking the support of Americans to discredit his own countrymen? Who gave foreign nationals the right to interfere in India’s internal affairs? We are more than capable of dealing with our own issues. We don’t need outsiders interfering in our country’s affairs," the CJP founder wrote. The American singer, however, did not back down and hit out at Dipke yet again. "The truth sets everybody free. Even you. And here’s the truth: these US donors will drop you like a hot cake when you don’t succeed. And you won’t, because lawlessness never wins. Instead, take your U.S. education, talent, and use it for good. Sit down with PM Modi and be a positive voice to advance India. The truth of your courage to do what’s right lies in your next steps," the singer wrote. Millben added that Modi did not need American support because he has " 1.5 billion beautiful Indian citizens who support him and have for 25 years, 12 years as PM, three consecutive terms. And will again in 2029. That’s the truth." Mary Millben is a prominent African-American Hollywood actress and singer. She became a known name in India for her rendition of the national anthem and religious song 'Om Jai Jagdish Hare'. Millben also sang the Indian national anthem at an event in 2023 during OM Modi's visit to the US. This is not the first time the singer has supported PM Modi. On completion of his 25 years in public service, Millben described the prime minister as a “shining beacon of the Indian dream”. She also called for unity across communities to mark the milestone. news.exam_corner_topic: Does India need stand-off missiles or more fighter jets?
news.headline: Does India need stand-off missiles or more fighter jets?
news.story_lead: Does India need stand-off missiles or more fighter jets? The Narendra Modi government,after Operation Sindoor,has realised that what India needs is proper anti-ballistic missile defence, long-range air-to-air missiles Outgoing Air Chief Marshal Amarpreet Singh in his last media interaction raised red flags over declining fighter force levels and called for the induction of two squadrons (36 aircraft) of fighters each year to maintain the Indian Air Force (IAF)'s might over its regional rivals. The chief hinted that fighter force levels were going down to 30 squadrons even though the Chief of Staff Committee (COSC) had mandated the strength to be 42 squadrons.
news.full_article_text: Does India need stand-off missiles or more fighter jets? The Narendra Modi government,after Operation Sindoor,has realised that what India needs is proper anti-ballistic missile defence, long-range air-to-air missiles Outgoing Air Chief Marshal Amarpreet Singh in his last media interaction raised red flags over declining fighter force levels and called for the induction of two squadrons (36 aircraft) of fighters each year to maintain the Indian Air Force (IAF)'s might over its regional rivals. The chief hinted that fighter force levels were going down to 30 squadrons even though the Chief of Staff Committee (COSC) had mandated the strength to be 42 squadrons. What the chief is saying has merits. But there remains another question: what will a manned Indian fighter do against Chinese PL 17 beyond visual range air-to-air missiles with a range touching around 400 km or air defence systems like S-400, which take out the fighter at the range of over 300 km. What is the efficacy of a fighter that can be shot out of the sky the moment it stabilises to launch an air-to-ground or air-to-air missile ? The Indian military may take comfort in the fact that it is well placed vis a vis Pakistan but its real adversary is China, which has achieved theatrization of commands, with much faster capacity to respond and with actionable intelligence. The Iranians with an air force not even worth the name have managed to stand up to US-Israel during seven months of war and have caused economic and political havoc in West Asia by targeting Gulf countries with unmanned combat air systems, cruise missiles, kamikaze drones and top of the line ballistic missiles. Iranian proxy, the Houthis, with no air force worth the name, have made life miserable for the Saudi-led Sunni Mecca alliance and has targeted Damman, Riyadh and East-West pipeline of the Kingdom with ballistic missiles. The Kingdom with American F-15, Tornado, Typhoon fighters have not been able to neutralise the Houthis but Saudi has plans to buy fifth generation US F35 fighters. The Houthi attacks have shown that Saudi does not have any anti-ballistic missile defence and its oil infrastructure is a sitting duck for Shia Houthi stand- off weapons. The Narendra Modi government, after Operation Sindoor last May, has realised that what India needs is proper anti-ballistic missile defence, long-range air-to-air missiles, long-range loitering ammunition, hypersonic ballistic missiles and long range kamikaze drones. Ukraine, with hardly any fighter force, is using ramped up drone capacities has been able to hit Russian energy infrastructure so much so that no oil refinery is functioning in the former superpower. Keeping in mind the need for long-range weapons, India is planning to acquire Russian RVV-BD air-to-air missiles with a range of around 300 km and integrate with Su-30 MKI fighters. It is developing Astra Mark II missile with a range of around 200 km with a test-fire scheduled this year. Astra Mark III will have a range of 300 km plus when its development is completed. India also will be getting 31 Predator high-altitude, long-range drones from US in 2028-29 with capacity to fire air-to-air missiles and heavy ordnance on ground. It is not about whether the Indian Air Force should or should not get its fighters but the efficacy of an expensive system in times of long-range missile and air defence systems. The age of tanks and dogfights is long over. India cannot spend money on systems like Pantsir to protect its tanks while its S-400 systems are under threat from enemy rockets and missiles. Given that the defence budget is not unlimited, the priority today is a strong anti-ballistic missile system with a considerable inventory of missiles, long-range air defence (India’s fifth S-400 system comes from Russia next month), long-range drones, rockets and missiles. Even the acquisition of a fifth generation fighter like Su-57 does not make sense given that the Iranians blew the much-touted stealth features of the F-35 to smithereens by using basic infra-red heat seeking missiles during the Iran war. The F-35 survived but its image got hit. India has to prepare for future wars with stand-off long-range weapons. For that, it will and is rethinking its military doctrines as even Pakistan is buying drones and long-range missiles in large numbers post-Operation Sindoor. What good is a fifth generation fighter if it gets shot out of the sky the moment it takes off by enemy air defence system. - ABOUT THE AUTHOR Shishir Gupta Shishir Gupta is Executive Editor at Hindustan Times and one of India's top journalists covering national security, strategic affairs, foreign policy and geopolitics. Over the past three decades, he has extensively reported on India's military, diplomatic and security landscape, covering every major conflict and national security challenge, from the 1999 Kargil War and the 2020 East Ladakh standoff to Operation Sindoor in 2025. He has also covered major terror attacks, including the IC-814 hijacking, the 26/11 Mumbai attacks and the 2025 Pahalgam terror strike, along with numerous Pakistan-backed terrorist incidents in the Kashmir Valley and across India. He has reported on national and state elections for more than three decades. A recognised authority on strategic affairs, Gupta has covered India's nuclear programme since the Pokhran-II (Shakti series) tests in May 1998 and has written extensively on global nuclear issues, Indian diplomacy and the country's expanding global outreach. He has also reported widely on international conflicts and terrorism, with a special focus on the Indian subcontinent. Gupta has interviewed Prime Minister Narendra Modi more than four times, including Modi's first interview with the print media after becoming Prime Minister in May 2014. His other interviews include three with the Dalai Lama, as well as conversations with Benjamin Netanyahu, Amit Shah, Yogi Adityanath, S. Jaishankar, Nirmala Sitharaman and Piyush Goyal. He is the author of Indian Mujahideen: The Enemy Within (Hachette, 2011) and Himalayan Face-off: Chinese Assertion and Indian Riposte (Hachette, 2014). He was awarded the Chevening-Wolfson Joint Scholarship at Wolfson College, University of Cambridge, UK, in 1998 and participated in the International Visitor Leadership Program (IVLP) of the US State Department in 2006. He received the Ben Gurion Prize from Israel in 2011 and the K. Subrahmanyam Prize for Strategic Studies in 2015 from the Manohar Parrikar Institute for Defence Studies and Analyses (MP-IDSA). Since 2024, he has hosted Point Blank, Hindustan Times' weekly YouTube show on global geopolitics. Read More

news.story_lead: Hindu converts to Islam can’t claim Muslim backward quota, rules Supreme Court The bench said a person’s pre-conversion social status does not automatically entitle them to affirmative action benefits after converting to a non-Hindu faith The Supreme Court on Thursday upheld a Madras High Court judgment striking down a Tamil Nadu government order that allowed individuals from backward classes and denotified communities who convert to Islam to claim reservation benefits Rejecting an appeal by the Tamil Nadu government, a bench of justices PK Mishra and Shree Chandrashekhar held that a person’s pre-conversion social status does not automatically entitle them to affirmative action benefits after converting to a non-Hindu faith. “A person who converts to Islam does not become part of the Muslim backward class category. A person’s pre-conversion status cannot confer on him the status of backw
news.full_article_text: Hindu converts to Islam can’t claim Muslim backward quota, rules Supreme Court The bench said a person’s pre-conversion social status does not automatically entitle them to affirmative action benefits after converting to a non-Hindu faith The Supreme Court on Thursday upheld a Madras High Court judgment striking down a Tamil Nadu government order that allowed individuals from backward classes and denotified communities who convert to Islam to claim reservation benefits Rejecting an appeal by the Tamil Nadu government, a bench of justices PK Mishra and Shree Chandrashekhar held that a person’s pre-conversion social status does not automatically entitle them to affirmative action benefits after converting to a non-Hindu faith. “A person who converts to Islam does not become part of the Muslim backward class category. A person’s pre-conversion status cannot confer on him the status of backwardness,” the bench said. The Tamil Nadu government had approached the top court against the high court’s verdict that scrapped a 2024 government order which allowed converts from backwards classes, most backward classes, denotified communities and scheduled caste to be issued community certificates of one of the seven notified backwards class Muslim sects. The state government had reasoned that the move was based on the recommendation of the Tamil Nadu Backward Classes Commission. The bench rejected the argument. “A person who is converting from a Hindu social order to non-Hindu social order cannot claim affirmative action under Article 16(4) of the Constitution merely on the basis of social backwardness associated with his pre-conversion status,” it said. The court was of the view that conversion severs the legal foundation of caste-based backwardness associated with the Hindu social order under Article 16(4) of the Constitution. The legal challenge originated from a petition filed by Paramasivam, a Hindu who converted to Islam in 2015 and adopted the name Sameer Ahmed. After local district authorities rejected his application for a Backward Class Muslim (BCM) certificate as a “Labbai” Muslim, he approached the high court. He argued that the Tamil Nadu Backward Classes Commission recommended in his favour and directed that Hindu backward classes who convert to Islam shall be treated as Backward Class Muslims and issued community certificates. The high court held that membership of a notified Muslim community, such as Labbai, Rowther, Marakkayar or Deccani Muslim, was determined solely by birth and could not be acquired by conversion. The court held that these communities represent distinct socio-cultural communities rather than theological sects, making entry via religious conversion legally untenable.

news.exam_corner_topic: Ensure Mahua Moitra can visit constituency without hurdles, Supreme Court tells Bengal govt ahead of Durga Puja
news.headline: Ensure Mahua Moitra can visit constituency without hurdles, Supreme Court tells Bengal govt ahead of Durga Puja
news.story_lead: Ensure Mahua Moitra can visit constituency without hurdles, Supreme Court tells Bengal govt ahead of Durga Puja The court also suggested that a protocol could be put in place for visits by MPs to their constituencies. The Supreme Court on Thursday asked the West Bengal government to ensure that Trinamool Congress MP Mahua Moitra receives the necessary cooperation from local authorities and police when visiting her Krishnanagar constituency, urging the state to make appropriate arrangements ahead of the Durga Puja and Diwali festivities. A bench of Chief Justice of India Surya Kant and justice Joymalya Bagchi told solicitor general Tushar Mehta, appearing for the state government, that while the state could take time to respond to Moitra’s petition, the MP should not face difficulties in visiting her constituency in the meantime.
news.full_article_text: Ensure Mahua Moitra can visit constituency without hurdles, Supreme Court tells Bengal govt ahead of Durga Puja The court also suggested that a protocol could be put in place for visits by MPs to their constituencies. The Supreme Court on Thursday asked the West Bengal government to ensure that Trinamool Congress MP Mahua Moitra receives the necessary cooperation from local authorities and police when visiting her Krishnanagar constituency, urging the state to make appropriate arrangements ahead of the Durga Puja and Diwali festivities. A bench of Chief Justice of India Surya Kant and justice Joymalya Bagchi told solicitor general Tushar Mehta, appearing for the state government, that while the state could take time to respond to Moitra’s petition, the MP should not face difficulties in visiting her constituency in the meantime. “You take your time to respond but if the MP wants to visit her constituency, let there be necessary arrangements,” said the bench, following which Mehta agreed to return on Friday with a statement on the arrangements that could be made. The court also suggested that a protocol could be put in place for visits by MPs to their constituencies, with the solicitor general agreeing that one should exist. “There can be a kind of protocol when MPs visit,” observed the bench, adding that the upcoming festivities made the issue pressing. “There must be some protocol. There are 800 MPs after all,” Mehta responded, to which senior advocate Gopal Sankaranarayanan, appearing for Moitra, retorted that the difficulties were being faced by only one MP. Mehta sought time to file his response, reiterating the Centre and state’s objection to the maintainability of the petition. The bench, however, made it clear that the question of maintainability would remain open while it considered the immediate concern over Moitra’s visits to her constituency. “Let this matter be taken up tomorrow,” said Mehta, with the bench agreeing to hear it on Friday. Moitra, who represents Krishnanagar in the Lok Sabha, moved the Supreme Court seeking guidelines to ensure that MPs receive the cooperation of local authorities and police while visiting their constituencies and carrying out development works under the Members of Parliament Local Area Development (MPLAD) scheme. The plea followed a series of incidents that she alleged had impeded her ability to discharge her responsibilities as an elected representative. One of the key grievances concerned her eviction from the Nadia Circuit House on the night of August 14, when, according to her petition, a large crowd had gathered outside the premises, abusing and threatening her, while her requests for police assistance went unanswered. The episode was followed by a September 1 communication from the Nadia district administration requiring MPs and MLAs to give advance notice of at least three to four days before seeking accommodation in government guest houses. The letter also stated that such accommodation would depend on the overall situation prevailing at the time. On October 1, the Supreme Court had sought responses from the West Bengal government and the Centre on Moitra’s plea, expressing concern over the district administration’s requirement that an MP inform it three days in advance before visiting the area and accessing the Circuit House. At the time, the bench had questioned the rationale for such a requirement, observing that an MP seeking to stay at a Circuit House was being asked to notify the administration three days beforehand. Moitra’s petition contends that state authorities cannot obstruct an elected representative from performing constituency-related duties or discriminate against a parliamentarian on the basis of political affiliation. It also seeks a framework to ensure that local officials remain impartial while facilitating MPs’ visits and development work. The state and Centre have challenged the maintainability of the petition, with Mehta previously cautioning that allowing an MP to bring personal grievances directly before the Supreme Court could set a precedent. news.headline: Code 7500: Mystery hijack alert forces Air India flight diversion
news.story_lead: Code 7500: Mystery hijack alert forces Air India flight diversion Flight AI 2030, carrying 306 people, was cleared to continue its journey after security agencies inspected the aircraft and crew. An Air India flight from Frankfurt to Delhi was diverted to Jaipur on Wednesday after air traffic control (ATC) received a hijack alert for the aircraft. Officials said the pilot told ATC there was no hijacking, and ATC asked him to divert to Jaipur.
news.full_article_text: Code 7500: Mystery hijack alert forces Air India flight diversion Flight AI 2030, carrying 306 people, was cleared to continue its journey after security agencies inspected the aircraft and crew. An Air India flight from Frankfurt to Delhi was diverted to Jaipur on Wednesday after air traffic control (ATC) received a hijack alert for the aircraft. Officials said the pilot told ATC there was no hijacking, and ATC asked him to divert to Jaipur. The Directorate General of Civil Aviation (DGCA) , India’s aviation regulator, will examine the ATC system for a possible technical error. Flight AI 2030, a Boeing 787-9 with 306 people on board, landed safely at Jaipur and was moved to an isolation bay for security checks. According to people aware of the incident, the aircraft was briefly squawking transponder code 7500, the internationally recognised aviation code for hijacking or unlawful interference. Airline and DGCA officials, speaking on condition of anonymity, said the flight was diverted on ATC’s instructions. The airline officials also said the pilots had made no mistake. Deep Dive Also read: Frankfurt-Delhi Air India flight diverted to Jaipur after hijacking alert, probe on Air India flight resumes journey to Delhi The aircraft was cleared to fly on to Delhi. It took off from Jaipur at 2.37pm and landed in Delhi at 3.11pm. In a statement, Air India said the flight was diverted “following a perceived security concern”, and that security agencies had checked and cleared the aircraft and crew. A passenger told HT that one of the pilots spoke to passengers about 30 to 40 minutes before the scheduled landing in Delhi, as the crew was preparing to begin descent from cruising altitude. “He said he didn’t know why, but he had been asked by ATC to divert to Jaipur and land there. He said he’d keep us updated,” said Swasti Rao, a professor at OP Jindal Global University and a consulting editor at The Print. Officials separately confirmed that the pilot told passengers the diversion was on ATC’s instructions. The crew came back on almost every 10 minutes after that, she said, telling passengers they were landing at Jaipur and were in touch with Delhi ATC. After landing, the pilot came back on the public address system. “I didn’t want to panic anybody, but there was a hoax,” Rao quoted him as saying. Also read: Air India cancels flights to and from Riyadh, Dammam, Jeddah until October 17 How aircraft transponders work A transponder is a radio receiver and transmitter on board an aircraft. It answers a ground radar’s ping with a four-digit code, which lets controllers tell one aircraft from another on their screens. Pilots and controllers call sending that code “squawking”. Each digit runs from 0 to 7, which allows 4,096 codes. In India, controllers assign each departing flight its own code. International flights entering Indian airspace keep the code they were using in neighbouring airspace, and an aircraft without an assigned code sets 2000 before it enters. Three codes are reserved worldwide: 7700 for an emergency, 7600 for radio failure and 7500 for unlawful interference, which covers hijacking. Under US rules, controllers never assign 7500 unless the pilot has first reported unlawful interference. On the Boeing 787 , pilots set the code through tuning and control panels (TCPs) on the flight deck’s centre console. These are units with a display and a keypad, which crews also use to tune radios and navigation aids. A pilot selects the transponder page and keys in the four digits. Controllers tell the crew which code to set, usually over the radio, and the crew enters it. Aircraft also broadcast their transponder code through ADS-B, a system in which an aircraft transmits its own position and status, and public flight-tracking sites pick up those broadcasts. Wednesday’s case was similar to a January 2025 incident when a Mumbai-bound Air India flight, which had just taken off from New Delhi’s Indira Gandhi airport , sent an emergency signal to air traffic control (ATC) in the Capital, suggesting it had been hijacked. The pilot later informed the ATC that it was a false alarm. Also read: 'Were told can't land in Delhi due to security reasons': Frankfurt-Delhi Air India passengers recall hijacking scare A possible glitch “The DGCA will investigate the ATC system for a possible technical error,” an official said, asking not to be named. A former bureaucrat offered one possible explanation, which he described as a hypothesis. “One possible explanation is a technical anomaly within the system that generates or assigns transponder codes, potentially involving multiple aircraft operating in close proximity during military formation flights. Aircraft may be assigned different codes, such as 7511, 0011 or 5600, and a system-level glitch could theoretically result in an unintended code combination that this time produced 7500, the internationally recognised hijack alert code. Similar anomalies have occurred previously, but they never resulted in the generation of 7500, thus not attracting this level of attention. However, this remains a technical hypothesis and would require verification through a detailed examination of the system, flight data and ATC records,” he said. India’s published air traffic rules say the pilot of an aircraft subjected to unlawful interference should try to set the transponder to 7500. Under international procedures, controllers who see the code do not mention unlawful interference on the radio unless the pilot does so first. They ask the crew to confirm the code, and India’s rules treat a pilot’s silence as confirmation that the code was set deliberately. - ABOUT THE AUTHOR Neha LM Tripathi Neha LM Tripathi is a Special Correspondent with the National Political Bureau of Hindustan Times. She covers the aviation and railways ministries, and also writes on travel trends. Her work spans national developments, with a focus on policy, people, and the evolving travel landscape. news.exam_corner_topic: CAPF Act doesn’t override Supreme Court’s 2025 verdict, IPS deputation necessary: Centre
news.headline: CAPF Act doesn’t override Supreme Court’s 2025 verdict, IPS deputation necessary: Centre
news.story_lead: CAPF Act doesn’t override Supreme Court’s 2025 verdict, IPS deputation necessary: Centre A home ministry officer, who filed the counter affidavit, denied that this was done to nullify the judgment or challenge the court’s authority. New Delhi: The Centre has defended the Central Armed Police Forces (General Administration) Act, 2026, in the Supreme Court, maintaining that it neither seeks to override the apex court’s May 23, 2025 judgment nor declares the ruling erroneous or void, while maintaining that the deputation of IPS officers to senior positions in the CAPFs is necessary for the country’s internal security architecture. In a counter affidavit filed on Wednesday, a day before a special bench is scheduled to hear petitions by serving CAPF officers challenging the law, the government said the Act did not re-enact any provision struck down by the court.
news.full_article_text: CAPF Act doesn’t override Supreme Court’s 2025 verdict, IPS deputation necessary: Centre A home ministry officer, who filed the counter affidavit, denied that this was done to nullify the judgment or challenge the court’s authority. In a counter affidavit filed on Wednesday, a day before a special bench is scheduled to hear petitions by serving CAPF officers challenging the law, the government said the Act did not re-enact any provision struck down by the court. It also said the law came into force on October 8 through a notification and that the cadre review exercise directed by the court was underway. “It is submitted that the 2026 Act came into force on October 8 by virtue of notification,” the joint affidavit filed on behalf of the Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA), the Department of Personnel and Training (DoPT) and the CRPF stated. The petition was filed by more than 800 serving CAPF officers, including Shaurya Chakra, Kirti Chakra and other gallantry award winners, who have challenged the law, arguing that it seeks to circumvent the apex court’s ruling. The bill was passed by Parliament in April despite opposition leaders raising concerns that it would undermine the morale of cadre officers. The Supreme Court’s May 2025 judgment had directed the Centre to progressively reduce IPS deputation to the five CAPFs — the CRPF, BSF, CISF, ITBP and SSB — up to the inspector general (IG) rank. The ruling followed an almost 16-year legal battle by CAPF cadre officers over promotional stagnation and the deputation of IPS officers to senior posts. The cadre officers have argued that large-scale deputation has restricted their promotional opportunities and prevented them from reaching leadership positions. They have also contended that while the court directed the government to progressively reduce IPS deputation, the new law prescribes fixed quotas for deputation at senior ranks. The government, however, said the recruitment rules of each CAPF had, “from their inception”, provided for the appointment of IPS officers on deputation. It rejected the argument that IPS officers lacked the competence to hold senior command positions, saying they served in internal security, counter-insurgency and left-wing extremism theatres, border districts and intelligence organisations. Denying that IPS officers occupied most senior posts, the government said 47 of the 607 sanctioned deputy inspector general (DIG) posts were held by IPS officers, while 64 of the 140 sanctioned IG posts were allocated to them. The affidavit said IPS officers brought knowledge of state administrations, police forces and regional security situations to CAPF leadership. They also acted as a key link between the Centre and state governments in policing, law and order, counter-insurgency, militancy, terrorism and border protection. The government further said the deputation quotas were “neither without any study nor without determining principle”, as alleged by the petitioners. On cadre review, the Centre said the exercise was underway within the framework of the 2026 Act. It also provided the dates on which proposals for cadre reviews of all five CAPFs were sent to the Department of Personnel and Training. Retired CAPF officers and their families have announced a peaceful protest against the Act at Jantar Mantar in November. - ABOUT THE AUTHOR Prawesh Lama Prawesh Lama, an Associate Editor at Hindustan Times with nearly two decades of frontline reporting experience across India’s conflict zones, border regions, and disaster-hit areas. He writes on internal security, insurgency, the Northeast, and Left-wing extremism and has reported from India’s hinterland and some of the most sensitive and strategically critical regions. news.headline: Pictured: Winning entries for Wildlife Photographer of the Year 2026
news.story_lead: - Published 14 October 2026, 00:26 BST An emotional scene of an elephant carrying a deceased calf has earned Italian photographer Federico Veronesi the title of Wildlife Photographer of the Year 2026. While tracking elephants in Namibia's Huab River Valley, Veronesi spotted an unusual trail of drag marks across the sand of a dry riverbed. Following the tracks, he came across a female elephant carrying a dead calf, its leg wedged between her tusk and trunk.
news.full_article_text: - Published 14 October 2026, 00:26 BST An emotional scene of an elephant carrying a deceased calf has earned Italian photographer Federico Veronesi the title of Wildlife Photographer of the Year 2026. While tracking elephants in Namibia's Huab River Valley, Veronesi spotted an unusual trail of drag marks across the sand of a dry riverbed. Following the tracks, he came across a female elephant carrying a dead calf, its leg wedged between her tusk and trunk. Initially, Veronesi assumed the elephant was the calf's mother. But after sharing his photographs with an elephant research project working in the area, he learned that this wasn't certain. Researchers recognised the elephant as a female who had lost a calf several years earlier and said she had previously picked up dead calves belonging to other females. For Veronesi, the encounter was deeply significant. "Of all the 20 years I've done photographing animals, this is the most heart-wrecking and fascinating and dramatic," he said, describing it as "revealing of the depth and complexity of the emotions, the feelings of the animals." He hopes the image will encourage people to look beyond animals' physical appearance and recognise them as individuals with their own relationships, memories and emotions. "It's a small window that opens just a crack into the complexity of their world," he said. The competition's annual exhibition , external opens at the Natural History Museum on Friday 16 October 2026. Keep scrolling to see more award-winning images. Labour of love Category : Young Grand Title and 11 to 14 Years Photographer : Oscar Whitfield, Zimbabwe/UK Location : Zambezi National Park, Zimbabwe Only by lying in the dust and capturing the beetle at eye level could Whitfield show how much strength its task required. While on a family game drive in Zimbabwe, near his home in Victoria Falls, he spotted the dung beetle struggling to push a ball of dung uphill through the sand, with a trail of flies following closely behind. After experimenting with different angles and compositions, he captured a moment that reveals the extraordinary effort involved in this seemingly simple task. "I hope that when people look at the photograph, they can see too, and maybe appreciate how much can be happening in a small moment in the natural world," says Whitfield. Flight of the Bumblebee Category : 10 Years and Under Photographer : Amelie Davis, UK Location : Surrey, England You do not need a camera or a plane ticket to take an award-winning photo. Davis captured this shot in the garden using her dad's smartphone. The image freezes in time a single wingbeat from a common carder bumblebee as it prepares to land on a flower. The Meeting Place Category : Animals in their Environment Photographer : James Lewin, UK Location : Chyulu Hills National Park, Kenya Lewin captured this dreamy, black-and-white photo of a young bull elephant spraying zebras at a waterhole. He softened the usually harsh light by using a camera converted to infrared. A Watchful Eye Category : Animal Portraits Photographer : Aaron Sanders, UK Location : Porthkerris Beach, Cornwall Common octopuses are usually found in the warmer Mediterranean Sea. But with global warming pushing up springtime sea temperatures, sightings across south-west England have massively increased. Sanders described the moment he spotted a single eye peeking from behind the kelp: "We remained perfectly still, watching one another with a seemingly shared curiosity." Scenes from the Swamp Photographer : Isak Pretorius, South Africa Location : Mabamba Swamp, Uganda Fewer than 5,300 mature shoebill storks are estimated to remain in the wild. Yet Pretorius, while canoeing with a guide, was able to capture these two â likely a breeding pair collecting material for their nest. Despite their name, shoebill storks are actually more closely related to pelicans, herons and ibises. Birdsong Painted in Light Category : 15-17 Years Photographer : Konrad GrÃ¤eter, Germany Location : Baden-WÃ¼rttemberg, Germany Spring sees male blackbirds search for high vantage points to sing and try to attract a mate. This photo was taken in a vineyard at dawn, when the birds sing their most complex compositions. Urban Jungle Category: Urban Wildlife Photographer: Seth Forestson, UK Location: Lumphini Park, Bangkok, Thailand Forestson lowered himself onto the mud to capture this common water lizard against the city skyline. These adaptable lizards live in cities across South and South East Asia and will take whatever food is available, such as catfish and koi. Making Morays Category: Under Water Photographer: Tony Wu, USA/Japan Location: Kagoshima Prefecture, KyÅ«shÅ«, Japan This is probably the first time the courtship ritual of Abbott's moray eels has been photographed, the NHM said. Wu worked with biologists and used dim red light and a customised fisheye lens to minimise disturbance. Wily Coyotes of San Francisco Category: Photojournalist Story Award Photographer: Loren Elliott, USA San Francisco is estimated to be home to around 100 coyotes, living alongside a large human population. While they can prey on domestic animals, they also help control disease-carrying rodents, and residents' attitudes towards them are mixed. Protective Pose Category: Behaviour: Amphibians and Reptiles Photographer: Anton Sorokin, US Location: Contra Costa County, California, USA Sorokin dipped his camera and lights in a murky pond to catch this glimpse of a California newt laying her eggs. Shifting Sand Category : Behaviour: Invertebrates Photographer: Sitaram Raul, India Location: Thar Desert, Rajasthan, India A scorpion is photographed burrowing into the shifting dunes of India's Thar Desert. Exploring the dunes at night, Raul saw many scorpions searching for prey but as temperatures rose after sunrise, the scorpion dug into the sand to escape the intense heat. Night-Time Catch Category: Oceans: The Bigger Picture Photographer: Alex Lindbloom, USA Location: Off Cenderawasih Bay, Papua, Indonesia A whale shark investigates the catch of a mobile net-fishing platform, known as a bagan. Lindbloom searched for sharks around dawn, using the bagan's bright lights to illuminate them when there was too little natural light for his drone. Shedding Light Category: Plants and Fungi Photographer: Agorastos Papatsanis, Greece Location: Litochoro, Pieria, Greece Papatsanis used ultrviolet light to illuminate mushrooms known as "beautiful bonnets" growing from a decaying log on the lower slopes of Mount Olympus in Greece. Hidden Depths Category: Rising Star Award Photographer: Alexis Tinker-Tsavalas, Germany Location: Germany and Northern Ireland, UK Tinker-Tsavalas uses macro photography to reveal the intricate details of tiny animals that are easily overlooked, particularly in urban habitats. His interest in macro photography developed during the Covid-19 lockdowns, when he was restricted to habitats close to his home in Berlin. Escape Artistry Category: Nat

An emotional scene of an elephant carrying a deceased calf has earned Italian photographer Federico Veronesi the title of Wildlife Photographer of the Year 2026.
While tracking elephants in Namibia's Huab River Valley, Veronesi spotted an unusual trail of drag marks across the sand of a dry riverbed.
Following the tracks, he came across a female elephant carrying a dead calf, its leg wedged between her tusk and trunk.
Initially, Veronesi assumed the elephant was the calf's mother. But after sharing his photographs with an elephant research project working in the area, he learned that this wasn't certain.
Researchers recognised the elephant as a female who had lost a calf several years earlier and said she had previously picked up dead calves belonging to other females.

For Veronesi, the encounter was deeply significant. "Of all the 20 years I've done photographing animals, this is the most heart-wrecking and fascinating and dramatic," he said, describing it as "revealing of the depth and complexity of the emotions, the feelings of the animals."

He hopes the image will encourage people to look beyond animals' physical appearance and recognise them as individuals with their own relationships, memories and emotions. "It's a small window that opens just a crack into the complexity of their world," he said.

news.full_article_text: Madras HC asks Tamil Nadu police why RSS annual route march permission is denied every year Madras High Court asked the Tamil Nadu police why the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS) was denied permission to hold its annual route march in the state The Madras High Court on Wednesday asked the Tamil Nadu police why the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS) was denied permission to hold its annual route march in the state, irrespective of the party in power. If the “State of Jammu and Kashmir” could allow meetings or marches by the RSS, “why Tamil Nadu can not have it?” Justice V Lakshminarayanan said. “What is your fear? Every year they (RSS) are coming (for permission) amd the Court is granting. What is so exceptional in 2026? Has there been any violence so far in their march?” the high court asked. “State is looking at citizens as enemies, what to do?” Justice Lakshminarayanan remarked, adding that successive governments had rejected such requests. The court was hearing a petition filed by RSS North Tamil Nadu secretary VG Jagadeesan, challenging police orders denying permission for marches scheduled across the state. Jagadeesan’s plea sought permission for RSS route marches on October 18 and 25 and November 1. The petitioner proposed that participants wear the organisation’s uniform and march alongside a musical band, followed by public meetings. Advocate general Vijay Narayan argued that the routes proposed for the RSS marches were unsuitable and that permitting the processions during the festive season would “inconvenience the public, particularly those out shopping for Diwali and Navratri.” Narayan said the marches would also require substantial police deployment at a time when the authorities had other responsibilities. The judge questioned the need for repeated litigation over permissions for processions and suggested that the state should enact legislation if it intended to prohibit them altogether. “Pass a legislation saying no person will be entitled to take a procession or a march if the State is insistent on denying permission,” the high court said. Senior advocate NL Rajah, appearing for the petitioner, argued that the RSS had conducted annual marches since its inception in 1925. He also submitted that procedural guidelines governing processions did not constitute inflexible statutory requirements and that the police should seek clarifications from organisers instead of rejecting applications outright. Rajah objected to police orders referring to mosques along the proposed routes, arguing that such reasoning undermined Tamil Nadu’s communal harmony. Justice Lakshminarayanan also said that the presence of places of worship along a route should not, by itself, justify refusing permission. Advocate general Narayan argued that the proposed routes were unsuitable and that the marches could inconvenience the public during the festive season. He also cited the substantial police deployment that the events would require. The court directed the petitioner’s counsel to meet state public prosecutor R John Sathyan on Wednesday to discuss the dates, timings and routes, and report the outcome on October 15. news.headline: Thousands march to Indian Supreme Court to demand election chief resign
news.story_lead: India's opposition party members march to the Supreme Court in protest against a controversial revision of voter lists that has sparked days of unrest, in Delhi - Published 12 October 2026 Thousands of opposition supporters marched through Delhi to India's Supreme Court to demand the election chief resign over alleged electoral roll fraud. Monday's "March for Democracy" was the latest in a series of demonstrations, with thousands of security forces deployed and roads barricaded in the capital. Thousands of protesters were detained over the weekend.
news.full_article_text: India's opposition party members march to the Supreme Court in protest against a controversial revision of voter lists that has sparked days of unrest, in Delhi - Published 12 October 2026 Thousands of opposition supporters marched through Delhi to India's Supreme Court to demand the election chief resign over alleged electoral roll fraud. Monday's "March for Democracy" was the latest in a series of demonstrations, with thousands of security forces deployed and roads barricaded in the capital. Thousands of protesters were detained over the weekend. Congress leader Rahul Gandhi submitted a petition to the court challenging the process, in which tens of millions of names have been struck off the voter rolls. Opposition parties allege the revision benefits Prime Minister Narendra Modi's ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP). The Election Commission and the BJP reject the charge. For weeks requests to protest had been denied by police, citing law and order reasons. Attempts to hold a protest by the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) pressure group over the weekend led to thousands of demonstrators being detained in Delhi. Gandhi called "all opposition parties, civil society groups [and] all those who believe in democracy" to join Monday's march. In a press conference, he shared a letter that he and Congress President Mallikarjun Kharge had written to Chief Justice Surya Kant, laying out their concerns with Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar's alleged conduct. After they filed their petition later in the day, Kant responded by saying the matter was already before the court and therefore sub judice - meaning he could not speak about it. But he added: "You have my assurance that any such petition shall be heard at the earliest possible opportunity, in accordance with the law." There was a heavy security deployment in central Delhi and along the route of the march, with restrictions on traffic and on entry and exit at some metro stations. A bus carrying Gandhi and other opposition leaders made its way to the court from Barakamba road. Supporters waved flags and chanted his name as the Congress MP and others waved through the windows. Seated a few rows behind him was Neha Bora, a student leader who has gained prominence in the protests. A few kilometres on, in a place called Mandi House, the bus stopped and Rahul Gandhi and a few others climbed on top of the vehicle to wave at supporters lining up the street in the thousands. Many protesters climbed on to other buses parked here, while some waved flags and chanted anti-government slogans to the sound of drums and lots of cheering. "If they take away our right to vote, what is left with us?" one protester asked an AFP news agency reporter. Another protester called the march "a fight to save the very fabric" of India, the world's largest democracy. Main opposition leader Rahul Gandhi holds up a copy of India's Constitution at a press conference on Monday Protesters have been demanding the country's the election chief resign over alleged electoral roll fraud Over the past week, top opposition leaders, including Gandhi, have been briefly detained several times while leading protests in central Delhi. On Sunday, the CJP - which is not a registered political party - said it would continue protesting until Kumar stepped down. The CJP, which successfully led a protest over the summer that culminated in India's federal education minister's resignation, had called for a march on Saturday to Jantar Mantar - the best-known protest site in Delhi where the last set of sit-in demonstrations had also happened. But authorities in Delhi imposed overarching restrictions that made it almost impossible for protesters to travel and reach Jantar Mantar - trains were cancelled, dozens of metro stations were shut and tens of thousands of police and paramilitary personnel were on the roads to detain protesters. The Home Ministry has now announced demonstrations will no longer be permitted at Jantar Mantar. Three other sites have been listed as alternatives should permission be granted. Monday's demonstrations come after thousands were detained over the weekend The CJP leaders - founder Abhijeet Dipke and co-convenors Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka - were dramatically detained from a plane as they landed in Delhi to join the weekend protest. They were only released a day later - while Dipke returned home to attend his grandmother's funeral, Das and Ranka held a press conference where they said the protests would continue. Both leaders have said they will seek a new protest date from the police. Over the weekend, the police detained and released thousands of people, including several journalists. Some videos and photos from the protest show police dragging people, including women, by force and pushing them into buses. The BBC also captured footage , external of a policeman slapping a detained protester inside a bus. The Delhi police did not respond to questions about the use of violence against protesters. In a statement, Reporters Without Borders condemned the detention of at least 16 Indian journalists. "Covering events of public interest is not a crime. It is their job. The police's actions against the press are unacceptable," it said. Rahul Gandhi said that young Indians who had come to peacefully protest with "love in their hearts, not hatred or anger" had been beaten up. BJP President Nitin Nabin accused opposition parties and the CJP of trying to destabilise India "at the behest of foreign forces" without elaborating on who the forces were. Related topics

Opposition parties allege the revision benefits Prime Minister Narendra Modi's ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP). The Election Commission and the BJP reject the charge. For weeks requests to protest had been denied by police, citing law and order reasons. Attempts to hold a protest by the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) pressure group over the weekend led to thousands of demonstrators being detained in Delhi. Gandhi called "all opposition parties, civil society groups [and] all those who believe in democracy" to join Monday's march. In a press conference, he shared a letter that he and Congress President Mallikarjun Kharge had written to Chief Justice Surya Kant, laying out their concerns with Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar's alleged conduct. After they filed their petition later in the day, Kant responded by saying the matter was already before the court and therefore sub judice - meaning he could not speak about it. But he added: "You have my assurance that any such petition shall be heard at the earliest possible opportunity, in accordance with the law." There was a heavy security deployment in central Delhi and along the route of the march, with restrictions on traffic and on entry and exit at some metro stations. A bus carrying Gandhi and other opposition leaders made its way to the court from Barakamba road. Supporters waved flags and chanted his name as the Congress MP and others waved through the windows. Seated a few rows behind him was Neha Bora, a student leader who has gained prominence in the protests. A few kilometres on, in a place called Mandi House, the bus stopped and Rahul Gandhi and a few others climbed on top of the vehicle to wave at supporters lining up the street in the thousands. Many protesters climbed on to other buses parked here, while some waved flags and chanted anti-government slogans to the sound of drums and lots of cheering. "If they take away our right to vote, what is left with us?" one protester asked an AFP news agency reporter. Another protester called the march "a fight to save the very fabric" of India, the world's largest democracy. Main opposition leader Rahul Gandhi holds up a copy of India's Constitution at a press conference on Monday Protesters have been demanding the country's the election chief resign over alleged electoral roll fraud Over the past week, top opposition leaders, including Gandhi, have been briefly detained several times while leading protests in central Delhi. On Sunday, the CJP - which is not a registered political party - said it would continue protesting until Kumar stepped down. The CJP, which successfully led a protest over the summer that culminated in India's federal education minister's resignation, had called for a march on Saturday to Jantar Mantar - the best-known protest site in Delhi where the last set of sit-in demonstrations had also happened. But authorities in Delhi imposed overarching restrictions that made it almost impossible for protesters to travel and reach Jantar Mantar - trains were cancelled, dozens of metro stations were shut and tens of thousands of police and paramilitary personnel were on the roads to detain protesters. The Home Ministry has now announced demonstrations will no longer be permitted at Jantar Mantar. Three other sites have been listed as alternatives should permission be granted. Monday's demonstrations come after thousands were detained over the weekend The CJP leaders - founder Abhijeet Dipke and co-convenors Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka - were dramatically detained from a plane as they landed in Delhi to join the weekend protest. They were only released a day later - while Dipke returned home to attend his grandmother's funeral, Das and Ranka held a press conference where they said the protests would continue. Both leaders have said they will seek a new protest date from the police. Over the weekend, the police detained and released thousands of people, including several journalists. Some videos and photos from the protest show police dragging people, including women, by force and pushing them into buses. The BBC also captured footage , external of a policeman slapping a detained protester inside a bus. The Delhi police did not respond to questions about the use of violence against protesters. In a statement, Reporters Without Borders condemned the detention of at least 16 Indian journalists. "Covering events of public interest is not a crime. It is their job. The police's actions against the press are unacceptable," it said. Rahul Gandhi said that young Indians who had come to peacefully protest with "love in their hearts, not hatred or anger" had been beaten up. BJP President Nitin Nabin accused opposition parties and the CJP of trying to destabilise India "at the behest of foreign forces" without elaborating on who the forces were. Related topics

news.headline: Supreme Court asks Centre, states to reply to plea seeking ban on sale of alcohol in tetra packs, sachets
news.story_lead: Supreme Court asks Centre, states to reply to plea seeking ban on sale of alcohol in tetra packs, sachets Nair said these tetra packs appear like fruit juice with alcohol content mentioned in smaller letters. The Supreme Court on Wednesday asked the Centre and states to file their response in four weeks on a plea for banning the sale of alcohol in "inconspicuous packaging" such as tetra packs and sachets. A bench of Justices Vikram Nath, R Mahadevan and Aparesh Kumar Singh gave the petitioner NGO 'Community Against Drunken Driving' two weeks to file its rejoinder thereafter and listed the matter for detailed hearing after six weeks.
news.full_article_text: Supreme Court asks Centre, states to reply to plea seeking ban on sale of alcohol in tetra packs, sachets Nair said these tetra packs appear like fruit juice with alcohol content mentioned in smaller letters. The Supreme Court on Wednesday asked the Centre and states to file their response in four weeks on a plea for banning the sale of alcohol in "inconspicuous packaging" such as tetra packs and sachets. A bench of Justices Vikram Nath, R Mahadevan and Aparesh Kumar Singh gave the petitioner NGO 'Community Against Drunken Driving' two weeks to file its rejoinder thereafter and listed the matter for detailed hearing after six weeks. Senior advocate Vipin Nair, appearing for the NGO, said alcoholic beverages being sold in tetra packs in 10 states and Union Territories (UTs) have deceptive imagery with names like 'Chili Mango Vodka'. He said these tetra packs appear like fruit juice with alcohol content mentioned in smaller letters. Nair said the Centre and states have not filed their response to the petition. The bench ordered, "Liberty is granted to the petitioner to serve the unserved respondents through the standing counsel for the concerned respondents... Four weeks' time is granted to the represented respondent(s) to file their counter affidavit(s). "The petitioner will have two weeks' time thereafter to file a rejoinder affidavit. List the matter after six weeks." The plea sought a direction to the Centre to frame a policy applicable to all states and UTs and to ban the sale of alcohol in packaging such as tetra packs and sachets. It also sought a direction to the Centre to frame a policy in respect of the states to amend their respective excise Acts, rules and policies forthwith, adopting uniform definitions of "bottling" limited to glass containers or other visibly distinct receptacles. The petition said there should be standardisation and harmonisation of excise policies of different states regarding the bottling of liquor. It said inconspicuous packaging had the potential to dramatically increase the public consumption of alcohol. "The petitioner is constrained to file this public interest petition after observing that alcohol, particularly cheaper alcohol, is being sold in inconspicuous packaging viz portable PET bottles, plastic sachets and tetra packs in various states across the nation," it said. Senior advocate Arvind Datar, appearing for Action Alliance for Recycling Beverage Cartons (AARC), sought impleadment of the petitioner and said that in the garb of a public interest litigation (PIL), the instant matter is specifically, directly and categorically targeted at the paper-based carton packaging industry since the entire petition has been premised on the argument that purportedly the sale of liquor in glass bottles is better than the sale of liquor in aseptic paper-based carton packages. The AARC said that liquor/ alcoholic beverages have been permitted to be sold in aseptic paper-based cartons in India for the past 21 years, and are presently so permitted in 10 states and UTs. "For example, the state of Karnataka has permitted such sales since 2005, the state of Andhra Pradesh since 2014 and the state of Uttar Pradesh since 2014. It is stated that state excise policies in this regard have been issued openly and in exercise of statutory power, and have continued uninterrupted since," it said. The plea of AARC said at present, an estimated 10 billion packs of alcoholic beverage cartons are being sold in India in a year. "It is stated that where a lawful practice has subsisted openly, under statutory permission, for almost 21 years, and where investment and employment on that scale have been created in reliance upon it, a petition seeking its prohibition without any explanation for the delay in challenging the same, is liable to be dismissed on the ground of delay and laches and more so where the relief would have an immediate and irreversible prejudice upon a large body of third parties not before the court," it said. The bench allowed the impleadment of AARC in the matter. The top court also asked the Centre and the states to file their responses in four weeks on the plea of the NGO for direction for an effective protocol and robust policy for the enforcement of mandatory age checks at liquor sales points. It directed that a copy be served to the office of Solicitor General Tushar Mehta for his response. "List the matter after six weeks. In the meantime, the petitioner may serve a copy of this petition in the office of the solicitor general. "Four weeks' time is granted to the respondent no. 1, Union of India, to file a counter affidavit," it said. On May 20, the top court sought responses from the Centre and other stakeholders on a plea for a ban on the sale of alcohol in tetra packs and sachets. On November 11, 2024, the top court sought a response from the Centre on a petition by the NGO which said that the excise policy of different states has age legislation making it illegal to consume or possess alcohol below a certain age but a robust mechanism to check the age of consumers or buyers at alcohol points of sale or consumption is absent. The petition has also opposed doorstep delivery of liquor service, contending it would hasten the formation of the habit of alcohol consumption among underage persons.

news.headline: Alcohol sold in tetra packs may mislead minors, Supreme Court seeks Centre’s response
news.story_lead: Alcohol sold in tetra packs may mislead minors, Supreme Court seeks Centre’s response The Supreme Court sought the Centre’s response to a PIL alleging that liquor tetra packs resembling fruit juice could mislead minors, encourage underage drinking and pose health risks. The Supreme Court on Wednesday sought the assistance of solicitor general Tushar Mehta in a public interest litigation (PIL) challenging the sale of alcohol in tetra packs, alleging that deceptive packaging resembling fruit juice could mislead consumers, encourage underage drinking and pose public health risks.
